subject: math

unit.title: Measurement: length, mass, capacity, temperature
unit.essentialQuestion: How do we measure and compare how long, heavy, full or hot things are?

title: Reading scales: mass and capacity
objectives: By the end, I can read a scale and choose the right unit for mass and capacity.

vocabulary.definition: a small unit for weighing light things
a big unit for weighing heavy things — 1000 g
vocabulary.example: a bag of potatoes weighs about 2 kg

vocabulary.definition: how much a container can hold
a big unit for liquids — 1000 ml
vocabulary.example: a big juice carton holds 1 litre

vocabulary.definition: the marked lines on a jug or weighing machine that we read
the jump between one mark and the next on a scale
vocabulary.example: each interval on this jug is worth 100 ml

emphasize: Read the INTERVALS first: work out what each mark is worth before you count marks — they're not always worth 1.
The big surprise: a taller container does NOT always hold more — trust the scale, not the shape.
Pick the unit that fits: grams for an apple, kilograms for potatoes; millilitres for a spoonful, litres for a big bottle.

keyConcepts: a scale's marks each stand for a set amount (intervals)
mass in g and kg (1 kg = 1000 g)
appearance vs measurement — height doesn't decide
misconceptions: the taller container holds more (judging capacity by height)
every mark on a scale is worth 1 — miscounting when intervals are worth 2, 5, 10 or 100
grams and kilograms (or ml and l) used interchangeably — 500 g called heavier than 1 kg because 500 > 1
hooks: Two containers — a tall skinny glass and a short fat cup. Which holds more? Let's pour and find out — it might surprise you.
priorKnowledge: reading numbers on a scale, like a ruler (Lesson 17)

human: a jug of coloured water (for visibility)
a tall thin glass and a short wide cup with the SAME capacity — test before the lesson!
three fruits to weigh (e.g. apple, banana, orange)
digital: jug-scale drawings on the whiteboard block

delivery.humanNotes: You run the first ~14 minutes with REAL kit (hook + explain + the reveal pour). Before the lesson: check that your tall thin glass and short wide cup really hold about the same amount; colour the water; keep the towel handy. The pour reveal in the example beat is the emotional heart of the lesson — let the child commit to a guess FIRST, then pour the tall glass into the wide cup. Keep the jug and scales in reach afterwards: the AI asks the child to weigh fruit and read jug levels during practice. When you say the handoff line after the reveal, the AI takes over.

video.watchTask: Every time a scale appears, work out what ONE mark is worth before the presenter says it — call it out first!

afterCheck.question: Before counting the marks on a scale, what must you work out first?

plan.goal: Get a committed guess on tall-vs-wide; retrieve reading marks from the ruler lesson.
plan.note: Don't pour yet! The guess must be locked in before the reveal in the example beat. Most children pick the tall glass — perfect.
plan.successCriteria: Child commits out loud to a guess and recalls that ruler marks stood for amounts we read.

script.say: Two containers — this tall skinny glass and this short fat cup. Which one holds more water? Tell me your guess and stick to it — we'll pour and find out later, and it might surprise you. Quick memory check from our ruler lesson: what did each little mark on the ruler stand for?
script.adaptHints: Write or repeat the child's guess back so it's locked in. Listen for 'a number / an amount we read'.

humanHandoff.setup: The tall glass and short wide cup side by side, empty; the jug of coloured water behind them.
humanHandoff.cueToResume: Not yet — the human continues into the explain beat.

stuckProtocol: If reading marks is shaky: hold the ruler next to the jug — 'same idea: marks with numbers, and we read where things reach.'

plan.goal: Model reading a jug scale by intervals (each mark = 100 ml) and introduce g/kg with a real weigh.
plan.note: Touch each mark as you count — the touching IS the method. Then the unit-size idea: 1 kg = 1000 g, grams for light things, kilograms for heavy.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees a pour read as '100, 200 — 200 ml' and hears that 1 kg = 1000 g, so 1 kg beats 500 g.

script.say: A scale has marks called intervals, and each one is worth a set amount. On this jug, each big mark is 100 millilitres. Watch me pour to the second mark — touch and count: 100… 200 — that's 200 ml. For heavy things we use grams and kilograms: 1 kg is 1000 g, so 1 kg is heavier than 500 g. We pick the unit that fits — grams for an apple, kilograms for a bag of potatoes. Let me weigh this apple… see the needle? Read what each mark is worth FIRST, then count the marks.
script.adaptHints: Let the child touch the jug marks as you count together. Keep the pour slow so the level visibly climbs mark by mark.

humanHandoff.setup: Jug filled to 200 ml, apple on the kitchen scales — both readings visible.
humanHandoff.cueToResume: Not yet — the human continues into the example beat (the reveal pour).

plan.goal: THE REVEAL: pour the tall glass into the short wide cup — same water. Then the child pours to the third mark and reads 300 ml.
plan.note: Maximum drama on the pour. Then hand the jug to the child: they pour to the third mark and read it themselves. End with the handoff line.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the tall glass's water fit exactly in the short cup, pours to the third mark, and reads 300 ml.

script.say: Now the big test. We filled the tall glass. Watch — I tip ALL of it into the short wide cup… it fits! Same water! The tall one LOOKED like more, but it isn't — the shape tricked our eyes. Height doesn't decide; measuring does. Your turn: pour water into the jug up to the THIRD mark. Touch and count the marks… what's the amount? … 300 ml! And one more: which is heavier — 1 kg or 500 g? — Brilliant. Now my friend on the screen has some scales for you to read. Watch!
script.adaptHints: If the child's guess was the tall glass, celebrate the surprise — 'your eyes tricked you, and now you know the trick!' Say the final sentence as written — it's the handoff.

humanHandoff.setup: The short wide cup holding all the tall glass's water; jug at 300 ml. Leave both visible as evidence.
humanHandoff.cueToResume: When the human says 'Watch!', the AI character starts the next beat.

stuckProtocol: If the interval count slips: put the child's finger on each mark and count together slowly — 100… 200… 300.

plan.goal: Diagnostic: 1 kg vs 500 g, and reading a jug at the second 100 ml mark.
plan.note: Probe after a correct read: 'How much is each mark worth?' — that question reveals whether the interval idea landed.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 1 kg (because 1 kg = 1000 g) and reads the jug as 200 ml by intervals.

script.say: Scale-reader's exam! First: which is heavier — 1 kilogram or 500 grams? … Second: look at my jug drawing. The marks go up in hundreds and the water reaches the second mark. How many millilitres? And tell me — how much is each mark worth?
script.adaptHints: If '500 g is heavier because 500 is bigger' comes up, don't correct directly — ask 'how many grams is 1 kg wearing when it puts its gram coat on?'

blocks.prompt: Which is heavier — 1 kg or 500 g?
options: 500 g, because 500 is a bigger number
blocks.explain: Match the units first: 1 kg = 1000 g. Now compare — 1000 g beats 500 g.

check.question: Which is heavier, 1 kg or 500 g? And read the jug filled to the second 100 ml mark.
check.expectedAnswer: 1 kg (= 1000 g); the jug reads 200 ml

wrongAnswers.why: compared bare numbers across different units
wrongAnswers.remedy: Put both in the same unit first: 1 kg in grams is…? NOW compare the numbers.

wrongAnswers.why: counted marks as worth 1 each — ignored the interval value
wrongAnswers.remedy: Each mark is worth 100! Touch and count with me: 100… 200.

wrongAnswers.answer: the tall glass holds more (if it resurfaces)
wrongAnswers.why: judging by height, not measurement
wrongAnswers.remedy: Remember our pour — the same water filled both! Height doesn't decide; the jug's marks do.

plan.goal: Weigh three fruits and order them; read two jug levels; pick sensible units — then a between-marks stretch.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank AND directs real actions ('weigh the banana — what does the needle say?'). On a miss, back to touch-and-count on the real jug (CPA step down).
plan.successCriteria: Child reads 2+ scales correctly using the interval value, orders the fruits by mass, and picks the right unit twice.

script.say: You're the scale-reader now! Three jobs: weigh your three fruits and put them in order, lightest to heaviest… read the jug levels I show you… and pick the right unit — would you weigh a strawberry in grams or kilograms? Remember the golden question: what is ONE mark worth?
script.adaptHints: React to the child's real fruit weights. Swap items for their interests — 'would you weigh your teddy in g or kg?'

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'I think the marks got counted as ones' or 'the shape tricked our eyes again.'
Go concrete: re-pour or re-weigh, touching each mark as you count together.
One hint: 'What is one mark worth?'
Re-ask an easier read (first mark = 100 ml), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child voices the surprise and the method; end on an earned success.
plan.note: Child-led recall — the character listens. The tall-glass story is the memory hook; let the child retell it.
plan.successCriteria: Child says taller doesn't mean more, and that you read what each mark is worth first.

script.say: So — what surprised you today about the tall glass? … Exactly: taller doesn't mean more — you have to measure! And what's the golden question before counting marks on any scale? … What is ONE mark worth. You trusted the measurement over how it looked — that's careful science-maths thinking.
script.adaptHints: Praise the observed process: committing to a guess and testing it, touch-counting intervals, matching units before comparing.

block.prompt: Which is heavier — 1 kg or 500 g?
block.explain: 1 kg = 1000 g, and 1000 g is more than 500 g.

wrongAnswers.why: compared bare numbers (500 > 1) across different units
wrongAnswers.remedy: The units are different sizes! Turn the kilogram into grams first: 1 kg = ? g. Now which number is bigger?

wrongAnswers.why: treats g and kg as the same unit
wrongAnswers.remedy: A gram is tiny — a raisin. A kilogram is a whole bag of sugar — 1000 grams! Which is more, 1000 g or 500 g?

hints: Put both in grams, then compare.

reteach.say: Same trick as pounds and pence: match the units before comparing. 1 kg puts on its gram coat — 1000 g. Now it's fair: 1000 g against 500 g. The kilogram wins — it's TWO 500s!

block.prompt: You want to weigh a strawberry. Which unit fits best?
block.explain: A strawberry is light — grams fit light things. Kilograms are for heavy things like potatoes. (Litres measure liquid, cm measure length!)

wrongAnswers.why: unit size not matched to object — a strawberry is a tiny fraction of a kg
wrongAnswers.remedy: A kilogram is a whole bag of sugar. Is a strawberry anywhere near that heavy? Which unit is made for light things?

wrongAnswers.why: mixed up mass and capacity
wrongAnswers.remedy: Litres measure how much a container HOLDS. We're asking how HEAVY the strawberry is — which family of units is for heaviness?

hints: Grams for light, kilograms for heavy.
Is a strawberry closer to a raisin or a bag of potatoes?

reteach.say: Units come in families and sizes. Heaviness family: grams for light things (a strawberry, a letter), kilograms for heavy things (potatoes, you!). Liquid family: millilitres for sips, litres for big bottles. Pick the one that fits the size of the thing.

block.caption: Match the unit to the size

block.prompt: A jug is marked every 100 ml. The water reaches the THIRD mark. How many ml?

wrongAnswers.why: counted marks as worth 1 each — ignored the interval value
wrongAnswers.remedy: Each mark is worth 100, not 1! Touch and count: 100… 200… 300.

wrongAnswers.why: muddled the mark count with the interval value
wrongAnswers.remedy: Don't mix them — every mark is a full 100. Count in hundreds: 100, 200, 300.

hints: First question: what is one mark worth?

reteach.say: Golden question first: what is ONE mark worth? Here — 100 ml. Now count the marks in hundreds, touching each: 100… 200… 300. Third mark, 300 ml. The mark's WORTH does the multiplying for you.

block.statement: The taller glass always holds more water than the shorter one.
block.explain: Remember the pour — the tall glass's water fitted exactly in the short wide cup! Width matters too. Only measuring tells you the capacity.

wrongAnswers.why: judging capacity by height — the lesson's key misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Think back to our pour: where did ALL the tall glass's water go? Did any spill out of the short cup? So does height decide?

hints: Remember the pour — did the water fit?
Tall and skinny can hold the same as short and wide.

reteach.say: Your eyes measure height, but water fills WIDTH too. The tall skinny glass and the short fat cup held exactly the same — we proved it with the pour. Shapes trick eyes; scales don't. When you want the truth, pour it into a measuring jug and read the marks.

block.caption: The pour test: same water, different shapes

block.prompt: Kitchen scales marked every 100 g. The needle points at the 4th mark. What's the mass?
block.explain: Each mark is worth 100 g: 100, 200, 300, 400. Four marks = 400 g.

wrongAnswers.why: counted marks as ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: What is one mark worth on these scales? 100! So count in hundreds: 100, 200…

wrongAnswers.why: right count, wrong unit — g/kg mix-up
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check the unit on the scale: it says grams. 400 g. How many g would it need to reach even 1 kg?

reteach.say: Every scale asks the same golden question: what is ONE mark worth? These scales say 100 g per mark. Needle at the fourth mark: 100, 200, 300, 400 — 400 grams. Not 4 — the marks aren't ones!

block.prompt: Sort these into the unit you'd measure them with.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: strawberry, letter, apple → g; potatoes, big dog, suitcase → kg

wrongAnswers.why: unit size not anchored — an apple is far less than a kilogram
wrongAnswers.remedy: A kilogram is 1000 g — a whole bag of sugar. Is one apple that heavy? Hold the thought of each in your hands.

wrongAnswers.why: grams over-stretched to heavy things
wrongAnswers.remedy: You'd need THOUSANDS of grams for a dog — that's exactly when we swap to kilograms. Light → g, heavy → kg.

hints: Lighter than a bag of sugar → grams.
As heavy as shopping bags → kilograms.

reteach.say: Use the bag-of-sugar test: a bag of sugar is 1 kg. Lighter than it? Weigh in grams — strawberry, letter, apple. As heavy or heavier? Kilograms — potatoes, a big dog, a stuffed suitcase. One quick imagine-it-in-your-hands and the unit picks itself.

block.prompt: Stretch! The jug is marked every 100 ml. The water sits exactly HALFWAY between the 100 mark and the 200 mark. About how many ml?

wrongAnswers.why: rounded down to the last mark — ignored the halfway position
wrongAnswers.remedy: It's PAST the 100 mark — half a jump more. Half of a 100-jump is…? Add it on.

wrongAnswers.why: muddled halfway with a bigger number / place-value slip
wrongAnswers.remedy: The water is between 100 and 200 — the answer must live between them. What number is exactly in the middle?

hints: Half of the 100-jump is 50 — add it to 100.

reteach.say: Between marks? Split the jump! The jump is 100, so halfway is 50 more. Water halfway past the 100 mark: 100 + 50 = about 150 ml. Scale-readers say 'about' when the level sits between marks — that's honest measuring.

wrongAnswers.why: borrowed £1 = 100p — wrong conversion
wrongAnswers.remedy: Close cousin, different family! Money: £1 = 100p. Mass: 1 kg = one THOUSAND grams. Kilo means thousand.

wrongAnswers.why: guessed a small conversion
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Kilo' is a power word — it always means a thousand. 1 kilogram = 1000 grams.

hints: It's more than £1 = 100p — one step bigger.

reteach.say: 'Kilo' is a secret code word meaning ONE THOUSAND. Kilogram = 1000 grams. (One day you'll meet kilometre = 1000 metres — same code!) So 1 kg = 1000 g, which is why it beats 500 g easily.

block.prompt: Ben says: 'The tall thin bottle must hold more than the short wide one — it's taller!' What would you tell him? How could you PROVE it?
block.sample: Taller doesn't mean more — the wide one might hold the same or more. Prove it by pouring each into a measuring jug and reading the marks.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Height doesn't decide capacity; pour both into a measuring jug and compare the readings

wrongAnswers.answer: Ben is right, taller holds more
wrongAnswers.why: the height-means-more misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Remember our tall glass — where did all its water fit? How could Ben test his idea instead of trusting his eyes?

wrongAnswers.answer: Just look really carefully at both
wrongAnswers.why: still judging by appearance, no measurement
wrongAnswers.remedy: Eyes got tricked last time! What tool turns 'it looks like more' into a number you can trust?

hints: What did our pour test prove?
Which tool gives you a NUMBER instead of a guess?

reteach.say: Tell Ben the scientist's answer: don't argue — measure! Pour the tall bottle into the jug, read the marks. Pour the wide one in, read again. Two numbers, and the bigger number wins no matter which bottle LOOKS bigger. We did it today: tall skinny glass and short fat cup — exactly the same water.

block.title: Prove it like a scientist
steps: Pour bottle 1 into the measuring jug — read the marks
Empty it. Pour bottle 2 in — read again
The number decides — not the shape!

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave mass, capacity and unit-choice items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach, then re-pour or re-weigh on the REAL kit touching each mark (CPA step down), then a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one interval read (marks worth 100) and one unit comparison (1 kg vs 500 g) → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'reading scales: mass and capacity'.
struggleProtocol: Name why (marks counted as ones / shape tricked the eyes / units mixed).
Go concrete: re-pour or re-weigh together, touching each mark as you count.
One hint: 'What is one mark worth?'
Re-ask an easier read (water at the first mark), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Weigh and measure the learner's own world — their teddy, their juice cup, ingredients for a food they love. Keep 'what is one mark worth?' as the constant question in every framing.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish with a read the child can win (first-mark read or the pour story retold), then specific process praise: what they DID (asked what a mark is worth, tested the guess, matched units) — never 'you're so clever'.

differentiation.support: Count the marked intervals aloud together, finger on each mark; coloured water for a crisp level; stick to marks-worth-100 with the water exactly ON a mark.
differentiation.stretch: Read a level halfway between marks ('about 150 ml'); convert 1 kg = 1000 g and use it to compare 750 g vs 1 kg; predict-then-weigh three fruits.

extension: Junior chef: measure out exactly 300 ml of water and 200 g of an ingredient (flour, rice) for a pretend recipe — both scales read by the child alone.
assessmentEvidence: Child reads mass and capacity scales using the interval value (including a between-marks estimate at stretch), compares 1 kg vs 500 g correctly, and rejects the height-means-more error with the pour as evidence.
revisitLater: Measures combine in Unit 8 problems — revisit reading scales then; bring back 'what is one mark worth?' as a retrieval starter; the interval idea returns with clock faces in Lesson 19 (each number = 5 minutes).
